description: No while/break/reduce_while or case in kernels, so algorithms like trial division scan the whole range (Elixir's Enum.all? stops early). Candidates: Enum.reduce_while-style {:cont, acc}/{:halt, acc} in for reduce, and case on integer literals.

comments.text: Early-exit syntax: Enum.reduce_while(enumerable, init, fn x, acc -> ... {:cont, acc} | {:halt, acc} end), plus Enum.all?/any?(enumerable, fn x -> bool end) as sugar over it. Rejected: {:cont, acc}/{:halt, acc} returned from a for ... reduce: clause. That is valid syntax but not early exit in Elixir: for/reduce has no halt protocol, so the tuple just becomes the next accumulator (for x <- 1..3, reduce: 0 do acc -> if x == 2, do: {:halt, acc}, else: {:cont, acc} end returns {:cont, {:halt, {:cont, 0}}}). Giving it halt semantics in kernels would make the same code mean different things in Elixir and defk. reduce_while is the stdlib's early-exit fold, carries tuple accumulators naturally, and its fn scope matches defk's for scoping. Enum.all?/any? cost ~10 lines as a desugaring and are what Elixir code actually writes for trial division (prime? = Enum.all?(2..limit//1, fn d -> rem(x, d) != 0 end)), so the Elixir baseline can use the identical call. find_index skipped (needs a nil/integer result, no nil in kernels). Enumerable: the same sources as a for generator (ranges with or without step, arrays). {:cont, _}/{:halt, _} must be literal tuples in every tail position of the fn body (through blocks, if/else, cond, case); anything else is a compile error. Halt is a goto to a label after that reduce_while's loop, so it exits only its own (innermost) loop; loops keep a single entry, so reducible resume (defk-nua) is unaffected.

title: Support early loop exit and case
